summary: This standards-track document specifies using DHCPv6 prefix delegation to give a mobile router prefixes for its mobile network. The mobile router is the requesting router and the home agent is the delegating router.

eli5.summary: A moving bus with Wi-Fi gets its own block of addresses from home base so riders' devices have them.

questions: how does a mobile router get a prefix
what is dhcpv6 prefix delegation for nemo
how does a mobile router get a prefix from its home agent
why does the mobile router use a dhcpv6 relay agent
subtitle: How a mobile router borrows DHCPv6 prefix delegation from its home agent to get the address blocks for its mobile network.

tldr.problem: A mobile router needs prefixes to assign to the links in its mobile network, and it needs them even while it is away from its home network.
tldr.mechanism: The home agent acts as the DHCPv6 delegating router and the mobile router as the requesting router. Away from home, the mobile router also runs a co-located relay agent so the messages can be unicast to the home agent, protected by IPsec.
tldr.outcome: Prefixes are handed out with the normal DHCPv6 exchange and then registered in the home agent's binding cache. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is not marked as obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 6276 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3633 and RFC 6275.

sections.title: Prefixes for a Moving Network
sections.content:
Network mobility support includes giving a mobile router a prefix or prefixes to use on the links in its mobile network. RFC 6276 specifies how DHCPv6 prefix delegation (DHCPv6PD, from RFC 3633) does this job.

In prefix delegation, a delegating router is given prefixes to hand out. A requesting router asks for them, the delegating router picks some and replies, and the requesting router is then responsible for those prefixes. The options from RFC 3633 are general-purpose and are not tied to mobile routers running the NEMO Basic Support protocol (RFC 3963).
sections.eli5: The moving network needs a block of addresses to give out to its devices. This RFC says to ask for them the same way any router asks its provider.

sections.title: Roles and Topologies
sections.content:
When the mobile router is at home, the home agent is the delegating router (the DHCPv6 server) and the mobile router is the requesting router (the DHCPv6 client). When the mobile router is away from home, it keeps the requesting router role and also becomes a DHCPv6 relay agent, co-located with the requesting router function.

The DHCPv6PD server at the home agent is provisioned with prefixes using any of the assignment mechanisms in the DHCPv6PD specification. Any other home agent state that must change as a side effect is left to the network mobility protocol. For NEMO Basic Support, the home agent adds a binding cache entry that registers the delegated prefix to the mobile router.

The key words MUST and SHOULD are used as in RFC 2119. The terms for Mobile IPv6 come from RFC 6275 and the DHCPv6 terms from RFC 3315 and RFC 3633.
sections.eli5: At home the mobile router just asks the home agent for addresses. Far from home it also acts like a mail forwarder so its request can travel back to the home agent.

sections.title: Away From Home
sections.content:
The mobile router MUST first register with the home agent by sending a Binding Update, and it MUST use implicit BU signaling, since it may not yet have requested any prefixes. Messages from the mobile router MUST carry the Home Address destination option, and messages from the home agent MUST use a Routing Header type 2, as RFC 6275 specifies.

If the mobile router has no active delegated prefixes (with unexpired leases), it MUST start with a DHCPv6 Solicit. The delegating router answers with Advertise, the mobile router sends Request, and the delegating router returns the prefixes in a Reply. If the router already has active prefixes, for example after a reboot or when the prefix is about to expire, it MUST start with a Rebind message.

The home agent selects the prefixes upon receiving the implicit Binding Update, unless they were pre-configured, and once the DHCPv6 signaling is done it MUST add an entry to its binding cache including the delegated prefixes.

Because the mobile router does not know its prefixes before it registers, it cannot derive its home address from one of them. It MUST assign its home address from the prefix on its Home Link.
sections.eli5: The mobile router first tells home base where it is. Then it asks for addresses, home base offers some, the router accepts, and home base writes down who owns them.

sections.title: The Relay Agent in the Mobile Router
sections.content:
A relay agent function MUST be used at the mobile router when it is away. The DHCPv6 client in the mobile router MUST hand every outbound message to the co-located relay agent, which wraps it in a Relay-forward message and sends it as a unicast packet from the mobile router's home address to the home agent's global unicast address. The relay agent MUST be configured to forward to the home agent, which is assumed to host the DHCPv6 server.

The relay agent sets these fields: msg-type is RELAY-FORW, hop-count is 1, and both link-address and peer-address are the home address of the mobile router. The options MUST include a Relay Message option and MAY include others.

Replies come back in a Relay-reply. The relay agent MUST extract the client's message from the Relay Message option and give it to the DHCPv6 client.

The RFC explains why it does not use the DHCPv6 Server Unicast option instead: the client would first need to receive that option, which needs a Solicit/Advertise exchange that itself requires a relay agent, so little would be gained.
sections.eli5: The relay is like an envelope. The client writes its request, the relay puts it in an envelope addressed to home base, and later opens the answer and hands it back.

sections.title: At Home, Home Agent Choice and Extras
sections.content:
When the mobile router is on its home link, the home agent MUST use the home link to exchange DHCPv6PD messages, and the co-located relay function MUST be disabled. Detecting this is left to the implementation, using the Home Link Detection mechanism in RFC 6275.

Not every home agent has to provide DHCPv6PD. A mobile router that needs it MUST find a home agent that does, by sending a Solicit asking for prefixes. If a home agent does not answer, or answers without delegating any prefix, the router concludes it lacks the service and keeps asking the other candidates. It is RECOMMENDED to set the Maximum Retransmission Duration and Count to non-zero values so the router stops after 6 Solicit messages, and RECOMMENDED to probe home agents one after another.

DHCPv6PD can be combined with the Rapid Commit option to get a two-message exchange. The same messages MAY also carry other DHCPv6 functions, such as assigning global addresses or passing a list of DNS recursive name servers (RFC 3646), and the home agent MAY act as relay agent for mobile nodes while serving as delegating router for mobile routers.
sections.eli5: If home base does not know how to hand out address blocks, the router asks six times, gives up, and tries another home base.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Two things are added to the security considerations of RFC 3315 and RFC 3633. First, the home agent must stop a mobile router claiming prefixes that belong to another one. On an implicit Binding Update, the home agent MUST only add prefixes to the binding cache entry if the router holds a valid DHCPv6PD lease for them, and MUST NOT add any otherwise. This also avoids forwarding traffic for prefixes not yet delegated.

Second, DHCPv6 here needs message integrity protection and source authentication. At home, ordinary DHCPv6 operation applies and nothing new is introduced. Away from home, the IPsec mechanism required by Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3776) MUST be used to protect the DHCPv6 signaling.

The RFC gives example Security Policy Database and Security Association Database entries in the format of RFC 4877, using ESP in transport mode for UDP traffic to and from the DHCP port. They are only examples, and other configurations are fine if they give the required protection. If the home address changes, the entries need to be re-created or updated.
sections.eli5: Home base only writes a block into its book if it really gave that block to this router, and the whole conversation is sent in a locked box.
